walkthroughs.body_html: The Compromise of 1850 strengthened slave-catching obligations even in free states. Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) galvanised Northern opinion. The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) and the Dred Scott decision (March 1857) widened slavery's possible reach. John Brown's Harpers Ferry raid (October 1859) electrified North and South.

Lincoln's November 1860 victory triggered Southern secession. Fort Sumter fell 13 April 1861. The Union Army numbered 2.1 million; Confederate 750,000-1,000,000. The Emancipation Proclamation (1 January 1863) redefined Union war aims. Gettysburg and Vicksburg (July 1863) shifted momentum. Lee surrendered at Appomattox on 9 April 1865; Lincoln was assassinated five days later.

The 13th Amendment (December 1865) abolished slavery. Black Codes provoked the Civil Rights Act (1866) and the 14th Amendment (1868). The Reconstruction Acts (1867) imposed military rule. The 15th Amendment (1870) banned racial voting barriers. KKK terror, the Slaughterhouse Cases (1873), the Civil Rights Cases (1883) and the Compromise of 1877 ended federal protection.

mcqs.q: What did Brown v Board of Education decide in 1954?
options: Lincoln ended segregation by signing the 14th Amendment.
Brown v Board of Education immediately desegregated all schools in America.
The Supreme Court ruled that 'separate but equal' schools were inherently unequal, overturning Plessy v Ferguson and beginning legal dismantling of school segregation.
Brown v Board ended slavery in the southern states.

mcqs.q: How did Malcolm X's approach differ from MLK's?
options: Malcolm X advocated violent terrorism against white Americans.
Brown v Board ended slavery in the southern states.
MLK preached nonviolent integration; Malcolm X (until 1964) advocated black self-defence, separatism, and rejected integration as a goal — though both shifted positions over time.
Malcolm X and MLK were close allies who jointly led the March on Washington.

mcqs.q: How was the US civil rights movement achieved?
options: Through decades of mass organising — NAACP legal work, grassroots campaigns, sit-ins, freedom rides — alongside leaders like King and Malcolm X.
Brown v Board ended slavery in the southern states.
Lincoln ended segregation by signing the 14th Amendment.
Martin Luther King's 'I Have a Dream' speech ended segregation.
